item.title: Elon Musk's megaphone propels conspiracy theory about James Talarico
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Elon Musk elevated a false conspiracy theory about Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico over the weekend, lifting a fringe claim concerning the Texan’s mental health to the forefront of users’ X feeds, where it garnered hundreds of thousands of impressions. “The Talarico campaign is hiding something big that voters ought to know about,” Musk wrote Sunday afternoon, replying to a post alleging that Talarico had been checked into the Lindner Center of Hope, a mental health facility in suburban Cincinnati. Musk’s reply amassed over 870,000 views, more than double the impression count of the post to which he was responding. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. The theory had been circulating online for days, fueled by Talarico’s absence from the campaign trail, which his team has consistently said was due to the flu. Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton promoted a “Tala-Freak-Out Tip Line” on Friday, which was still active as of Monday night. President Donald Trump weighed in, arguing the Democrat’s convalescence was too long to be the “flu bug.” Musk’s engagement with the theory gave it a much wider audience - and the flurry of attention ultimately prompted the treatment center in Mason, Ohio, to publicly refute the allegations. “Rep. James Talarico has never received treatment from Lindner Center of Hope,” the facility wrote in a statement posted to X, five hours after Musk’s initial posts on the subject. Talarico replied to the post Monday, saying he had “never even been to Ohio,” with a laughing emoji. A day earlier, he described the conspiracy theory as “the craziest thing I’ve ever heard” in an interview with MS NOW. Talarico’s spokesperson, JT Ennis, said the claims were a “lie designed to promote a pathetic conspiracy theory.” The episode demonstrates a key way that Musk is wielding political power in the midterms. He has retreated from the political spotlight after his public feud with Trump in 2025. He has taken a lower-profile approach to political spending this election cycle. He has used his formidable war chest to quietly back efforts to elect Republicans to office. The New York Times reported on Monday his midterm spending has swelled to at least $276 million since the beginning of July, making him the Republicans’ top individual donor. But on X, the social media platform he bought in 2022 and later folded into SpaceX, Musk continues to be outspoken about candidates and political issues - and his enormous audience acts as an influence machine, propelling a fringe claim into the political conversation with a single post. “You have someone … who is in bed with the political party, or an agenda, and is spreading falsehoods about an opponent who is gaining a tremendous amount of traction,” said Danielle Citron, a University of Virginia law professor who has spent more than a decade researching and writing about online abuse and has advised campaigns on the subject. “It is like a thumb on the scale that we haven’t really ever seen.” The Lindner Center of Hope and Musk did not respond to requests for comment. The theory surrounding Talarico originated in far-right circles, spreading further when right-wing influencer Nick Sortor posted an audio clip. The clip, which he claimed was a clinic employee stating that Talarico had recently been discharged, received 7.3 million views according to X. Sortor called for the Texas Democrat to quit the race. Talarico’s campaign said the candidate had been recovering from the flu, leading to a nine-day absence from the campaign trail. He appeared at an Austin music festival on Friday, even though the call that Sortor posted was recorded on Saturday night, according to phone logs posted by the caller. The conspiracy theories drove mentions of Talarico among key right-wing figures - including politicians and influencers - to their highest rate on record, a Washington Post analysis found. Until last week, Musk had posted relatively infrequently on Talarico - just twice in the past year. Since Wednesday, however, Musk has posted about Talarico at least a dozen times. One of Musk’s posts Sunday, a repost to his more than 240 million followers, put the onus on Talarico to clear the record: “If this was not true, Talarico’s campaign would immediately authorize the release of the records to clear him.” While Sortor’s audio clip led discussion to peak between 1 and 2 p.m. on Sunday, Musk weighed in as the matter was driving a significant level of conversation in right-wing circles - and it continued to hold traction for about eight hours afterward. Jared Holt, a senior researcher at Open Measures, a platform that measures the spread of online extremism and disinformation, said Musk’s elevation helped claims like Sortor’s proliferate. “His engagement with posts promoting the claims did boost them to wider audiences than they may have reached otherwise and likely served to legitimize them in the eyes of ideologically aligned users,” Holt said in an email. This kind of public attention can prove dangerous for ordinary figures suddenly lifted to the center of public fascination, he added. “The ecosystem where these claims spread has regularly elicited threats to schools, medical facilities, election offices, courts, and private businesses,” Holt said. Since buying the site formerly known as Twitter in 2022, Musk has regularly injected high-profile misinformation into users’ feeds. Late last year, Musk elevated allegations that members of the Somali-American community were involved in widespread fraud. Some rogue X users followed the posts from participants in the fraud claims to real life locations. Musk has also spread baseless theories about a volunteer in a Thai cave rescue, California wildfires and other topics. In 2022, shortly after acquiring Twitter, Musk elevated a conspiracy theory about Paul Pelosi, the husband of former Democratic House speaker Nancy Pelosi, who was badly injured in an attack at the family’s San Francisco home after a hammer-wielding intruder broke in and struck him in the head repeatedly. The rapid spread of online theories can place political campaigns in a tricky situation. Zac Petkanas was Hillary Clinton’s rapid response director during 2016 campaign, when online conspiracy theories alleged Clinton was secretly seriously ill and had to employ a body double to replace her on the campaign trail. “The way that it mattered [to Clinton’s campaign] was not that people believed Pizzagate or other conspiracy theories; it’s that it contributed to a narrative that she was potentially untrustworthy,” Petkanas said. “It was sort of a death by 1,000 paper cuts, and that was partly because people were really having to judge information coming off of the internet and realizing the scale at which misinformation could be weaponized. It’s 10 years later. People are much more inured to that.” Citron, the University of Virginia law professor, said actors take advantage of the short windows between campaigns and elections to spread falsehoods because they are unlikely to face consequences. If a claim is defamatory, for example, she said, the matter can take too long to resolve in the courts to have an impact on the race. “Given we’re within 30 days of an election, I think your lawsuit is not doing anything for you,” she said. “They know they’re in that chokepoint where you can tip an election. … It’s timed just right.” - - - Graphics: Right-wing attention on Talarico spiked on Sunday Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/10/13/fringe-theory-about-james-talarico-went-viral-then-elon-musk-weighed/

item.title: Trump's midterm challenge grows as gas prices rise and his approval falls
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
[BBC] Americans head to the polls on 3 November to decide how the rest of Donald Trump's presidency will play out. Thousands of races are taking place across the US, at different levels of government. But the main event for voters will be electing members of the House of Representatives and the Senate, the two chambers that make up Congress. Both of them are currently controlled by the Republicans, the president's party. The success or failure of Trump's final two years in office could rest on the outcome. Here's our visual guide to where the battle for power will be won and lost - from approval ratings, to key races and issues and the huge amount of money being spent. Midterms come at bad time for Trump One of the reasons the opposition Democrats have a chance to take back Congress is the president's low approval rating, which is a good indicator for how well his party could perform. He began his second term as president with an approval rating of just over 50%, according to polling resource website Silver Bulletin, but it quickly fell into the 40s. Trump's approval has fallen since taking office BBC It was hovering around 42% when Trump decided to launch air strikes with Israel against Iran at the end of February this year but it fell below 40% shortly afterwards. It is currently sitting at about 37%. Eight years ago, Trump's approval rating was significantly higher at this point in his first term, at 43%. Joe Biden's at the same point in his term was at 40%. In both cases, the sitting president lost control of the House in the midterms but kept hold of the Senate. But Trump's poor ratings help explain why Democrats are hopeful of winning both chambers of Congress and why they are setting their sights on states that Republicans have won consistently in recent years. The battle for the House The current Republican majority in the House of Representatives, the lower chamber, is as thin as it gets - they have 218 representatives, which is the exact number needed to have control, plus one independent who votes with them. The battle for the House Members of the House serve a two-year term so all 435 seats are up for election in November. But most districts are not considered competitive because the party that holds them has such solid support that there is only one likely winner. The Cook Political Report, which analyses campaigns and elections, suggests that just 21 districts are "toss-ups" that could be won by either party. Competitiveness of races Of those 21 toss-ups, 15 are currently held by Republicans and six by Democrats. If the Democrats win five of those on top of 28 districts classed as likely or leaning Democratic, they will win the House. Districts considered toss-ups Districts considered toss-ups Historically, the midterms see a high number of seats changing hands in the House, usually in a protest against the White House. The average number lost by the president's party is 27, according to data going back to 1934. Of those 23 elections, the president's party has only made gains in three. The battle for the Senate The Republicans have a slightly stronger hold on the Senate. They hold 53 of the 100 seats while the Democrats have 45 and two independents who also vote with them. The battle for the Senate Members of the Senate serve six-year terms so roughly a third are up for election every two years. Thirty-five seats are up for grabs in November but analysis by the Cook Political Report suggests that only seven of them are toss-ups that could go either way. Competitiveness of races Of those toss-ups, six are currently held by Republicans and one by Democrats. The Democrats would need to win four of those seats, plus the four classed as likely or leaning Democratic, to hit 51 and take control of the Senate. States considered toss-ups But winning a majority is no easy task for the Democrats. They need to keep hold of their seat in Michigan, where polls suggest the race is tighter than Democrats would like between Abdul El-Sayed, a left-wing political outsider, and his Republican rival Mike Rogers, a Trump ally and former FBI agent. And they would also need to pick up seats in states that Trump won by double-digits in 2024, including Alaska, Iowa and Ohio. But polls suggest they have a chance, even in Texas where former teacher James Talarico could become the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state since 1988 if he defeats Ken Paxton, the current state attorney general and close Trump ally. [BBC] GUIDE: What are the US midterms? EXPLAINED: What would Democratic control of Congress mean for Trump? IN DEPTH: The Republicans walking a Trump tightrope What are the key issues for voters? Trump pledged to "end inflation and make America affordable again" in his 2024 election campaign but the cost of living crisis is proving to be the key issue for voters. The president proudly declared that gas was "now below $2.30 [£1.74] a gallon in most states" in his State of the Union address on 24 February. But the war with Iran began four days later, disrupting Middle Eastern energy supplies and causing gas to hit $4 (£3.03) in the US. Changes in the price at the pump The war became increasingly unpopular as its consequences reverberated around the world and ultimately hit American consumers in the pocket. One poll carried out in August found 63% of respondents disapproved of Trump's handling of the situation. Other issues that voters say are important to them include healthcare and immigration. Trump has recently touted his policies around immigration as a big success, citing significantly lower border-crossing figures than in recent years. Many Democratic candidates are focusing on the high costs of US health insurance and the impact of Trump's legislation on access to the healthcare system. Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work? Can Trump defy political gravity? Most signs point towards a successful midterms for the Democrats, but it wouldn't be the first time that Trump and his party have outperformed polls if they do win more seats than expected. One of the few things in their favour is their huge financial advantage. At the end of August, the Republican National Committee and its allied groups had more than $600m (£455m) cash on hand, while the Democrats had just under $400m (£303m). On top of that, the Republicans also had more than $400m held by Trump's MAGA Inc group, the main fundraising and spending arm of the "Make America Great Again" political movement. Republicans have a financial lead The Republicans are using that financial advantage to buy advertising. More than $1bn worth of political ads were broadcast to US voters in September, according to research firm AdImpact . Republicans spent $200m more than the Democrats and outspent them in nearly all of the Senate races classed as toss-ups. Trump will be hoping this late messaging blitz can help convince Republicans to get out and vote in November, boosting turnout and limiting the damage done to him and his party. Whatever the result, attention will quickly turn to the next presidential election in 2028. Trump's unpopularity has dominated the midterms, but with him constitutionally unable to run for a third term the focus will shift to what the Democrats stand for, not just what they stand against. [BBC] Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here . Those outside the UK can sign up here . This article originally appeared on BBC at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/where-us-midterm-elections-won-050249260.html

item.title: Despite pushback from both parties, Trump defends his diesel deal with Russia
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Steve Holland WASHINGTON, Oct 12 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump on Monday defended a diesel oil deal he made with Russia as lawmakers from both parties complained the agreement appears to violate US law barring imports of Russian energy until Moscow ‌ends its aggression against Ukraine. Trump has said the deal to lift sanctions on Russian oil exports would help bring down high fuel ‌prices. However some analysts doubted the amount of diesel Trump has said Russia would provide over the next three months would do much to bring down prices, since it ​is equal to about 12 hours of global consumption of the fuel. On Friday, Trump said Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets, and his administration temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel designed to deprive Moscow of revenue for its war on Ukraine. On Monday, Trump said the deal would help American farmers and ranchers. The price of diesel has surged more than 60% since Trump launched a war against Iran seven months ago, and high prices ‌have jeopardized Republican chances to maintain thin majorities ⁠in the US Congress in the November 3 midterm elections. On Sunday a group of Republican and Democratic US senators called on Trump to "reverse course" on the diesel supply deal with Russia. They said his deal may violate a ⁠2022 law designed to support Ukraine in its bid to repel Russian invaders. "We should be tightening sanctions further, not undercutting them by allowing the import of Russian diesel and risking erasing our leverage, damaging our credibility with allies, and emboldening our adversaries," said Republican Senator Jerry Moran in a social media post. Trump has ​blamed ​Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries as a leading factor for higher diesel ​prices. "I made the right choice for the American People — ALWAYS, ‌AMERICA FIRST! President DONALD J. TRUMP," Trump said in a social media post. On Monday, Trump rejected criticism of the deal from members of his own party, in comments to reporters as he departed the White House on a trip to Ohio. "Well, I think these are Republicans that can't really be serious," he said. "We can do a restriction on oil, but the rest of the world would be greatly, greatly affected if we do that." Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy bickered over the weekend about the Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries. Trump said Ukraine needs a new president ‌and Zelenskiy promised to hold elections if Russia would agree to a 60-day ceasefire. Trump ​on Sunday declared that Russia and Ukraine agreed to halt attacks on each other's energy ​infrastructure. Whether such a deal will hold was unclear. "Well, they agreed," ​Trump told reporters. "They agreed because I said they agreed. ... That war has to be over with." Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov ‌said contacts were proceeding about a possible energy ceasefire ​as announced by Trump. He declined to ​comment on whether the ceasefire would apply only to oil refineries. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said Kyiv favoured a ceasefire, but both sides had to observe it. He said it was "increasingly clear" that Russia was unwilling to accept it as Moscow hit six Ukrainian energy ​facilities on Monday Zelenskiy told Fox News' "America's Newsroom" program ‌on Monday that Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries were not the leading cause of rising fuel prices. "Everybody understands that the prices on ​diesel — it doesn't depend on our attacks on diesel in Russia. Everybody understands that it depends on the blocking... the ​Strait of Hormuz," he said. (Reporting By Steve Holland; Editing by David Gregorio) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/trump-defends-russia-diesel-deal-152736373.html

item.title: Trump said Russia agreed to an energy ceasefire. Attacks on Ukraine's power grid continued.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Emergency services responded to a Russian drone strike on a residential building in Kharkiv, north-eastern Ukraine on Monday [EPA] Russia struck six Ukrainian energy facilities hours after US President Donald Trump announced the two countries had agreed to an energy ceasefire, Volodymyr Zelensky has said. Despite Trump stating on Sunday the truce would be "effective immediately", the Ukrainian president said Russia had hit "our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities". There were blackouts in the city of Izyum after a Russian strike destroyed power grids, Ukraine's state news agency Ukrinform said, while energy and railway infrastructure in western Ukraine was also targeted overnight. On Monday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring. What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim? Zelensky backs Trump's 'energy ceasefire' but says Russia continues to hit power plants Zelensky said 33 people had been injured in the strikes on energy facilities across the country. He told Fox News: "We did not attack, while Russia attacked our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities." "I think it was Putin's answer to President Trump," he added. Global conflicts have pushed fuel prices higher ahead of the US midterm elections and on Friday Trump announced a plan to import Russian diesel into the US on Friday. On Monday, Ukraine's state-owned grid operator Ukrenergo reported "new power cuts" in Kharkiv, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia due to damage caused to energy equipment by Russian attacks. Electricity rationing has been introduced in parts of Ukraine to avoid overloading damaged equipment, Ukrenergo said. Zelensky said on X the strikes were proof Russia was "unwilling to accept an energy ceasefire". On Monday evening, Kyiv's mayor Vitali Klitschko posted on Telegram that a drone hit a 25-story residential building in the Darnytskyi district. Several cars in the building's courtyard were also on fire, he said, with one person dead and 11 injured. Watch: What could Trump's energy ceasefire claim mean for Ukraine? When Trump first announced the ceasefire on Sunday , Zelensky said it was "news to him" that a truce was in effect, but he backed the proposed ceasefire as a "major step toward ending the war, if the Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect the energy ceasefire". Asked about the ceasefire on Monday, Trump said they agreed "because I said you agree", adding that the war "has to get settled". "That war is a disaster if you see the numbers," he said. For months, Ukraine and Russia have been exchanging strikes on energy infrastructure , disrupting energy supplies on both sides. Moscow has said the installations it hits are legitimate targets as they support Ukraine's military operation, while Zelensky has characterised Ukrainian attacks deep inside Russian territory as part of an effort to "reduce Russia's ability to finance the war". Analysis by BBC Verify on both Ukrainian and Russian strikes during the war have found both sides have increased their attacks in the lead up to the next winter. In 2026, BBC Verify has recorded 273 strikes on Russian-controlled oil and gas facilities, more than double the 124 recorded over the same period in 2025. Separately, analysis of data aggregated by global conflict monitor, the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project (Acled), recorded 2.4 times as many reported Russian attacks affecting Ukraine's energy network so far this year. Energy facilities in Kharkiv were hit by Russian strikes on Sunday evening, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said [EPA/Shutterstock] Trump has been urging Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian oil infrastructure, so Russia can fulfil the recently struck deal to release diesel to the US and the global market. The deal temporarily undoes US sanctions on energy imports, which Zelensky described as a "gift" to Russian President Vladimir Putin. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain "strongly supports President Trump's call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now", while France, Canada and the EU also expressed support. However, there has been a mixed response among European officials. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc would welcome an energy ceasefire "when it holds". Kallas said at a meeting of EU foreign ministers on Monday: "We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it." Meanwhile, Estonia's foreign minister said the ceasefire was "not working". Additional reporting by Benedict Garman, BBC Verify This article originally appeared on BBC at https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cvlyd4pdlwkxo?xtor=AL-72-%5Bpartner%5D-%5Byahoo.north.america%5D-%5Bheadline%5D-%5Bnews%5D-%5Bbizdev%5D-%5Bisapi%5D

item.title: Behavior rules for off-duty U.S. troops in Japan under review after Okinawa woman's death
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Officials are reviewing the off-base code of conduct for U.S. troops in Japan following the killing of an Okinawan woman, allegedly by a U.S. Marine , Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi said on Tuesday. Crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-runs and drunk driving by U.S. military personnel have long triggered protests on the southern Japanese island, which has for years urged other regions of the country to share the burden of hosting U.S. troops. "We plan to hold discussions including whether the existing rules are effectively functioning," Motegi said, adding that "matters such as patrols and curfew management" would be under review in talks with the United States. The high-level bilateral consultations will examine off-duty conduct and the "liberty" policy governing off-base private activities of U.S. military personnel, he said. The existing policy, updated in 2024 following a string of sexual assaults by U.S. military personnel in Okinawa, includes a ban on them drinking in public off-base between 1 a.m. and 5 a.m. or going to bars during those hours. Japanese police arrested a U.S. Marine stationed on Okinawa early this month on suspicion of killing a 39-year-old woman at a hotel in Naha, the capital of Okinawa Orefecture. Word of the arrest drew outrage . The U.S. military enacted a two-day operational pause after the Marine's arrest to reinforce discipline and standards, followed by a monthlong midnight-to-5 a.m. curfew. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Tuesday that "we began high-level, working-level consultations between Japan and the United States last week on what effective measures should be taken." "The Japanese government will continue to do everything in its power both to address this case and to ensure that it does not happen again," she told a legislative committee session. Motegi spoke by phone over the weekend with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who offered his "sincere condolences" over the alleged crime and pledged U.S. cooperation in the investigation. Crimes committed by U.S. personnel have long been a thorn in relations between the close security allies. A Japanese court sentenced a U.S. Marine accused of choking and attempting to rape a woman in her 20s to seven years in prison last year . In 2017, a former U.S. Marine and civilian military base worker was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa. The United States has approximately 54,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, mostly on Okinawa. This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/okinawa-us-troops-off-duty-behavior-rules-japan-review-womans-killing/

item.title: Apple's newest device is entering a market Amazon conquered years ago
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
After months of rumors, Apple is officially (and finally) making its biggest effort yet to grab a piece of the smart home pie. The iPhone maker announced the $299 HomeView on Tuesday, its first smart hub designed to put Siri front-and-center in people's homes. HomeView comes as a countertop device, or a slab you can mount to the wall, both with touchscreens, cameras and the ability to hear and execute Siri voice commands. This is Apple's first dedicated smart home hub ever, and it supports the numerous reports suggesting the company wants to make inroads in the home space. HomeView is designed to be stationary, and it not only connects all of your compatible devices together — things like smart lights, door locks and sensors (including the new Apple Home Collection ) — but also lets you control them using either the on-screen interface or Siri voice commands. But Apple may have a hard time convincing people to add yet another iPad-like screen to their homes, particularly one that emphasizes Siri. The new Siri, known as Siri AI , had a much delayed rollout and is only now available to users with the latest iPhones and devices running iOS 27 . Previously, Siri wasn't the most convenient voice assistant to use, nor the most helpful . Apple has a long way to go to catch up to the likes of Amazon's Alexa and Google's Assistant (now Gemini), and to make up for years of Siri being just meh. Plus, it's very late to the smart display party. To give credit where credit is due: Apple has certainly made progress with Siri. The new Siri AI is better at answering questions with greater detail than before, and it can include personal information from your calendar, Messages and other apps in its answers. This will likely come into play with the HomeView’s ability to recognize different users by their faces via the built-in camera and present personal information to them. But doing things that Alexa and Google have been able to do for a long time is just table stakes at this point. People barely want to use Siri on their iPhones; Apple not only has to prove Siri AI is good enough for people to want to use, period, but now it also has to show it's good enough to justify a separate, $299 device. With continuously skyrocketing tech prices , this may be a particularly tough sell. The fact that Apple is so late here is also working against the company. Amazon's original Echo Show came out in 2017, and Google's first Nest hub debuted in 2018. This isn't the first time Apple came into a space late of course — it has a habit of doing that and still coming out on top — but launching a device like this in 2026 feels a bit stale. Smart home hubs remain important for those building out connected spaces with dozens of devices, but plenty of smart home gear works over Wi-Fi now, no hub required. Privacy could be a selling point for HomeView, and it's an area where Apple has excelled in the past. Indeed, Apple is already emphasizing the privacy aspects of HomeView: the device runs on the A18 chip and includes Secure Enclaves, which are protected and compartmentalized, and process camera and microphone data. According to Apple, data processed by Secure Enclaves "cannot be accessed by the HomeView software, apps, the user, or Apple." Siri requests on HomeView can make use of on-device processing as well as Private Cloud Compute. Apple’s $299 HomeView is available for pre-order today, and will be widely available on November 13. This article originally appeared on Yahoo Tech at https://tech.yahoo.com/home/breaking-news/article/apples-new-siri-infused-homeview-hub-might-be-too-little-too-late-134206236.html

item.title: Trump targets Rep. Ilhan Omar and Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed at Ohio rally
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump went after Rep. Ilhan Omar hours after federal agents searched her home in Washington, D.C. (Kent Nishimura / AFP via Getty Images) Chants of “deport” rang out Monday night as President Donald Trump criticized Rep. Ilhan Omar , D-Minn., and Abdul El-Sayed , the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, at a rally for Republican candidates in Youngstown, Ohio. “I don’t know what they’re doing with it, but I can tell you this: She’s a disaster,” Trump said of Omar, whose home in Washington, D.C., was searched hours earlier by federal agents , two people familiar with the investigation told NBC News. A Justice Department spokesperson said in a statement that Homeland Security Investigations “executed a judicially authorized search warrant” as “part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation.” The statement did not specify that the investigation was related to Omar, nor did it provide more information about the search. “She comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military, where all they do is shoot each other, and she comes into our country and she says, ‘I have a constitutional right,’” Trump said. “She’s telling us about the Constitution, and she comes from one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet.” Trump then spoke of Somali gang activity in Minnesota and what the FBI has described as a recently thwarted shooting at the state’s Mall of America, alleged to have been plotted by an American-born U.S. citizen of Somali descent, The Associated Press reported . That’s when the first wave of “deport” chants began. Omar, who was born in the war-torn country of Somalia, immigrated to the U.S. as a child decades ago. El-Sayed was born in Michigan to Egyptian immigrants. “For 10 years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns,” Omar wrote earlier Monday on X . “This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.” Speaking to reporters Monday afternoon, Trump said he had “nothing to do” with the search of Omar’s home. At the rally, he segued from his attack on Omar and people of Somali descent in Minnesota to an attack on El-Sayed. “These people are crazy,” Trump said. “You look at the guy running in Michigan. He’s a jihadist.” Trump went on to praise El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, before he again referred to El-Sayed as a “jihadist” and proclaimed that “Somalia bandits, Third World gangsters, jihadist sympathizers do not belong in Ohio.” He added: “They don’t belong in America. Better get them the hell out of here.” More chants of “deport” then erupted from the audience at Youngstown’s Covelli Centre. A spokesperson for El-Sayed’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday night. Last week, after Trump referred to him on social media by his middle name, Mohamed, El-Sayed condemned it as a tactic meant to raise fears about his religion. “They point to my name and they point to my faith, trying to distract us from the challenges that we have,” El-Sayed, who is Muslim, told supporters at an event Thursday in Grand Rapids, Michigan. “My name did not raise your gas prices. My faith is not the reason you can’t afford your groceries.” Trump’s remarks Monday continued his leading role in ratcheting up rhetoric around Muslims and immigrants. Days after El-Sayed won Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary, Trump warned that the U.S. could become a “jihadist-run country.” And Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., accused El-Sayed of sympathizing with Osama bin Laden as he was campaigning with Rogers last week in Michigan. His last trip, to the Dayton area, included remarks about nearby Springfield. During a 2024 presidential debate, Trump repeated the unsubstantiated and racially charged claim that Haitian immigrants in the city were eating pets. item.title: Trump says he's 'looking at' firing Kimberly Guilfoyle as U.S. ambassador to Greece
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump answered he's "looking at" firing Kimberly Guilfoyle when asked about the embattled U.S. ambassador to Greece on Monday. Trump told reporters as he left the White House for a campaign rally that his administration is "looking at it" and added that it's "not happy" over reports alleging that she used her official position and links to the Trump family to get money from a donor . A Trump donor told ABC News last week that Guilfoyle offered access to top Trump officials in exchange for cash. Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images - PHOTO: Kimberly Guilfoyle, President Trump's nominee to be the US ambassador to Greece, speaks alongside President Donald Trump, during a Greek Independence Day celebration in the East Room of the White House in Washington, March 24, 2025. Eric Deters, a former lawyer, conservative media personality and Trump donor, alleged that Guilfoyle asked him to pay her $100,000 credit card bill in July 2025 -- days before her Senate confirmation hearing. Trump donor accuses Kimberly Guilfoyle of asking him to pay her $100K credit card bill: 'It was all quid pro quo' "It was all quid pro quo," Deters claimed about the request from Guilfoyle, who is the former wife of California Gov. Gavin Newsom and ex-fiance of Donald Trump Jr. The Wall Street Journal first reported on Deters' accusations. Deters provided messages to ABC News he says he exchanged with Guilfoyle on the subject. In one message from that period, Deters alleges Guilfoyle wrote, "Honey please I need you to get this done for me today," which Deters alleged was in reference to the desired credit card payment. ABC News has reached out to Guilfoyle, her attorney and the U.S. Embassy in Greece for comment and have not heard back. In a statement released late Sunday, Guilfoyle's lawyers claimed that the money she was seeking was for appearances and speaking engagements that predate her nomination that have not been paid, according to The Associated Press. Deters denies he owed Guilfoyle any money. He said he ended up not making the payment because he didn’t have the money. Deters is considered a controversial character in Kentucky politics. He ran for Kentucky governor in 2023 and to represent Kentucky's 4th Congressional District in the House in 2024; he lost both races in the primaries. A former lawyer, Deters had his law license suspended in 2012 for actions in multiple cases including comments he made about a judge and improper solicitation of a possible client. In refusing to reinstate Deters' law license in 2021, the Kentucky Supreme Court said he had a "notorious propensity" for filing "malicious or frivolous lawsuits," according to court documents. Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images - PHOTO: President Donald Trump speaks with reporters before walking to board Marine One on the South Lawn of the White House, Oct. 12, 2026, in Washington. In a statement to the Wall Street Journal, the U.S. embassy in Greece said Guilfoyle's "career in and out of public service is guided by deep and abiding values" and "the Ambassador remains committed to representing the American people with dedication and integrity." Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he wouldn't answer questions about Guilfoyle's alleged conduct last week while departing Athens, Greece. "I don't even know if it's true or not true," Rubio said. "So it's just not going to work that way, and it will certainly not going to work that way when I'm sitting in another country." But White House and State Department leadership have held discussions on how to address the allegations against Guilfoyle, including possibly dismissing her, according to two sources familiar with the matter. Both sources cautioned, however, that no final decision had been made; one source said the the president would have final say over any action. Several officials close to Rubio have expressed their frustration with Guilfoyle, whose reported misconduct loomed over Rubio’s high-profile visit to Athens last week. Guilfoyle was present throughout the secretary’s program in Greece, even appearing at some events that she had not been invited by the State Department to attend, one U.S. official said. The official said that the State Department’s inspector general is examining claims of possible misconduct by Guilfoyle, but it is unclear if a formal probe has been launched and the department has declined to publicly comment on any investigation. ABC News' Jay O'Brien contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on ABC News at https://abcnews.com/Politics/trump-firing-us-ambassador-greece-kimberly-guilfoyle/story?id=137209661

item.title: Houthi official warns of 'swift and painful response' if U.S. joins war in Yemen
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
This screen grab taken from CCTV footage released by the Saudi media ministry shows the moment King Khalid International Airport was hit by a strike (-) A Houthi official on Monday warned the US it would receive a "painful response" if it entered the war in Yemen, where Saudi Arabia has reportedly requested Washington's help in dealing with the group as it weathers repeated attacks. Yemen's civil war -- in which a Saudi-led military coalition supports the government against the Iran-backed Houthis -- reignited in July, months into the wider regional conflict that has roiled energy markets and plunged the Middle East into risis. The Houthis quickly began targeting Saudi oil facilities, tankers and transport hubs, including a string of lethal strikes on Riyadh's airport, rocking the world's top oil exporter. Blasts resounded over the capital again on Monday night, with the Saudi coalition saying it had intercepted a Houthi missile and the group saying it had again targeted the airport. Later, the coalition announced that it had intercepted two ballistic missiles in the south of the kingdom, near the border with Yemen. In a statement posted on X, the coalition said it had "intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Khamis Mushait", a city where a Saudi military base has previously come under attacks. Following an attack at the Riyadh airport on Saturday that killed 13 people, US President Donald Trump said he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the group, after having reportedly rebuffed previous requests for help from the kingdom. "The Houthis are misbehaving very badly. They're misbehaving very badly. No good," Trump said on Monday. "If the US becomes involved in the aggression against Yemen, we will not deliberate over the decision to respond, rather, there will be a swift and painful response targeting the US and all its interests in the region," Houthi political bureau member Mohammed Al Bukhaiti told AFP in an interview. He also warned "all employees and workers at Saudi oil facilities and airports to stay away from these sites, as they have become legitimate targets". Saturday's strike on King Khalid International Airport was the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in more than a decade, and also left hundreds wounded. Trump said the attack was "not acceptable" and that he would be speaking to the kingdom's de facto leader Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, telling reporters the US was "going to look at" the possibility of joining Saudi strikes. Operations remained suspended at the sprawling airport on Riyadh's outskirts on Monday. - 'Serious' response - Bukhaiti said the purpose of the campaign against Saudi targets was to send a message to the crown prince "that he can no longer wage aggression against Yemen from a safe position". Saudi energy minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman told a conference in Riyadh on Monday that the recent events had "tested our infrastructure, our institutions, our people, and our resilience". "The events of recent weeks are serious, our response must be equally serious." CCTV footage of Saturday's attack released by Saudi authorities showed Muslim pilgrims in religious attire waiting in departure lounges before a sudden blast tore through the building and brought down flaming debris. The atmosphere in Riyadh remained tense on Monday, as state broadcaster Al Ekhbariya said the military coalition was responding to drone and missile threats. In the evening, mobile phones received a loud government alert warning of a "hostile aerial threat" before the announcement of the interception. The alert delayed the kickoff of a football match between Uzbekistan's Neftchi Fergana and Saudi team Al Nassr, home to Portuguese superstar Cristiano Ronaldo. It was the first use of the phone alert system in Riyadh in weeks, with no official reason given for the lack of messaging during the attacks targeting the capital in recent days. The Houthis said they had also targeted the Khamis Mushait base in the kingdom's south with a drone. - Flights suspended - The US embassy in Saudi Arabia said US government employees must obtain its authorisation before using any airport in the kingdom, and urged US citizens to "take extreme caution" if they chose to do so. The mission also said "American citizens have been detained for taking photos of recent events" in Saudi Arabia. The UAE's national carrier Etihad Airways announced on Monday that it was cancelling all flights to and from Riyadh until next week, and also suspended flights to Dammam and Jeddah. Bahrain's national carrier Gulf Air said it too was cancelling all Riyadh flights until Saturday. US operator Delta announced it would delay the launch of direct flights from Atlanta to Riyadh, scheduled for October 23. Despite vast spending on military hardware, the Houthi attacks on oil, military and transport facilities across the large, mostly desert country are stretching Saudi defences. Thomas Juneau, security analyst at Ottawa University, said that despite some success, "Saudi Arabia is so large that it's simply impossible for them to consistently defend themselves". Riyadh leads an international coalition that has supported Yemen's government militarily since 2015, including by seeking to exert control over Yemeni airspace and the airport in the Houthi-held capital Sanaa. Juneau said the Houthis now "want to do to Saudi Arabia what Saudi Arabia does to them". The long-running Yemeni civil war has created a deeply entrenched humanitarian crisis in the impoverished country. UN rights chief Volker Turk said he was "appalled by the repeated attacks" on Saudi Arabia, but urged both sides to back down, adding "continued fighting will only unleash further misery with no end in sight". burs/ach/pdw This article originally appeared on AFP at https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/articles/saudi-says-resilience-tested-vows-134140110.html

item.title: Selma Blair appears emotional in court as lawyer explains what led to flight altercation
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
NEW YORK (AP) — Actor Selma Blair was arrested after she was accused of injuring two flight attendants on a trip from Los Angeles to New York. She was also accused of kicking a police officer taking her to the hospital and kicking a nurse once she got there. She pleaded not guilty Monday night to two counts of assault for state charges involving the officer and the nurse. And she faces separate federal charges based on what happened on the flight, which her representatives say was brought on by a severe medical emergency. Blair, 54, was detained by police at around 11 p.m. Sunday after the Delta Air Lines jet parked at the gate at John F. Kennedy International Airport, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey said in a statement. Blair and one of the flight attendants were taken to a hospital for evaluation, the Port Authority said. A police officer taking her to Jamaica Hospital Medical Center said in charging documents that while she was securing Blair to a stretcher, Blair pulled a leg from the straps and kicked her repeatedly around the face, neck and chest, causing serious pain and substantial swelling. Later, a nurse moving Blair said the actor kicked her in the chest, causing substantial pain. She was arraigned on two counts of second-degree assault late Monday at a court in Queens, where her lawyer entered a not guilty plea on her behalf. She appeared to cry as she stood in court in handcuffs, wearing jeans and a white hooded sweatshirt. Her attorney Shawn Barnes told a judge her actions were not intentional. He said the actor, who has multiple sclerosis, missed several doses of "a powerful medication that controls severe neurological symptoms," according to the New York Daily News and New York Post. He said she had gotten on the flight in Los Angeles after a heavy workload, and hit her head during the flight. He said these factors along with the altitude led to "a state of severe confusion and disorientation." The judge set her bail at $20,000 cash or $60,000 bond and set the next hearing for January. She left court with her lawyers. Details of what happened aboard the aircraft weren't immediately disclosed by the airline, police or the FBI, which was investigating, but Delta said in a statement it "has zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behavior, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first." In air traffic communications, the Delta pilot asked the tower to have medical personnel waiting at the gate to treat bite marks and a bloody nose, but said ambulances were not necessary. "It sounds like the disruptive passenger also bashed her head on the bulkhead or something like that," the pilot told the tower, according to audio posted on the ATC app. "So we'll obviously have to get her potentially checked out as well as involved with law enforcement." The FBI also issued Blair a notice charging her with assault related to her actions aboard the aircraft, according to a federal law enforcement official who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to speak publicly about the matter. Those charges will be handled through the petty violations court in federal court in Brooklyn. No date has been set for Blair's appearance. It's not the first time Blair has had issues aboard a plane. In 2016, Blair apologized for making statements she later regretted during a flight from Cancun to Los Angeles. She said she had mixed alcohol with medication, causing her to black out. Blair had major roles in films including 1999's "Cruel Intentions," 2001's "Legally Blonde" and 2004's "Hellboy." In recent years, she has advocated for disability rights after getting her multiple sclerosis diagnosis in 2018 . In 2023, she joined President Joe Biden at the White House to celebrate the anniversary of the Americans with Disabilities Act. ___ Yamat reported from Las Vegas and Dalton from Los Angeles. AP Transportation Writer Josh Funk contributed to this report. The White House has asked Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece, to resign amid allegations of improper conduct, Katie Zacharia, President Trump's new press secretary , announced on Tuesday. I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service." The Wall Street Journal reported last week that Guilfoyle asked a Trump donor to pay off a $100,000 American Express credit card bill ahead of her confirmation as ambassador in exchange for access to administration officials. Guilfoyle, 57, was confirmed as U.S. ambassador to Greece in September 2025. According to the Journal, as Guilfoyle was preparing for her Senate confirmation hearings, she asked Eric Deters, a former Kentucky gubernatorial candidate and Trump donor, to send a $100,000 wire transfer to help pay down her American Express account "in a way that wouldn't leave a paper trail." The report cited text messages between Guilfoyle and Deters. "Honey please I need you to get this done for me today," she texted Deters, according to the Journal. A lawyer for Guilfoyle told the Journal that she disputed the authenticity of the messages. Kimberly Guilfoyle speaks as President Trump listens at a Greek Independence Day reception at the White House in 2025. "Yeah, we're not happy." After the Journal’s report was published, Deters told NBC News that he viewed Guilfoyle’s request as a “quid pro quo.” "She was so desperate for that $100,000. It was a quid pro quo," Deters said. "She said I could ask her for anything and everything in Trump world. There was no request too big.” This is a breaking news story. Refresh this page for updates. item.title: Apple debuts HomeView hub as it reinvents smart home strategy
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Apple ( AAPL ) is reinventing its smart home strategy with its new HomeView hub, the HomePod Mini 2, and Apple TV 4K . Sporting a seven-inch Liquid Retina Display, the HomeView is designed to sit on a counter in its built-in speaker mount or be mounted to a wall. The $299 HomeView is designed to serve as the home base for your smart home and goes on sale Nov. 13. According to Apple, HomeView can recognize up to six household users via facial recognition and serve up their specific apps, notifications, and more. It can also play music and podcasts, make FaceTime calls, or look up quick video recipes in the kitchen. Users can control smart home devices ranging from lights and locks to thermostats and more, check their calendars, and interact with Siri AI to do things like find their keys via AirTags. Apple has dipped its toes into the smart home space over the years, including with the original HomePod, HomePod mini, and Apple TV, as well as software like its Home app, but has never offered a full-fledged hub like the HomeView before. Read more: 'I'm going to keep winning by innovating': Ring founder Jamie Siminoff isn't sweating Apple's smart home push Apple HomeView Apple Apple ceded much of the smart home space to rivals Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ) and Amazon ( AMZN ), which sell their Google Home and Amazon Alexa hardware lines. But the HomeView could change that. There are a number of do-it-yourself smart home options that allow users to set up a control center for their devices by mounting iPads on them. But the HomeView should provide a far easier, more cohesive offering for everyday consumers. Apple is also launching a new line of accessories built in collaboration with LG Electronics ( 066570.KS ) and Schneider. Called Apple Home Collection, the devices include a new LG in-home camera that can monitor your home and then turn the camera to face down when you enter the house for privacy. An outdoor camera can monitor deliveries and remember familiar faces. An LG door camera and lock can recognize your iPhone as you approach and quickly let you inside. Setting up the devices is as straightforward as connecting a pair of AirPods. Apple is marketing the Home Collection to individuals seeking products that easily integrate with the company's ecosystem and offer robust privacy features. The HomeView will be a major test for newly minted CEO John Ternus, who took over the top spot from Tim Cook on Sept. 1 and is reportedly angling to focus more on hardware and design. In addition to the HomeView, Apple also unveiled the $149 HomePod mini 2. Complete with new colors and Siri AI integration, the HomePod mini 2 allows you to do things like add events to your family calendar and ask about broad world knowledge. The $299 Apple TV 4K sports a more powerful processor and built-in far-field microphones that let you speak directly to the set-top box instead of holding down the remote's microphone button. You can also ask the Apple TV 4K where the remote is, and it will play a sound to help you find it if it slips between the couch cushions. item.title: Trump's spree of new projects mirrors his run-up to the 2018 midterms
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Trump has been appearing around the US in the run-up to the midterm elections, announcing economic development projects — from a possible pipeline in Alaska to a steel plant in Iowa to an aluminum smelter in Oklahoma — that he says will transform the country. "In the real economy, we are blowing it away," he said at a weekend stop in Tennessee . Trump's message of confidence comes as the ultimate shape of these projects remains far from certain and often directly echoes his pitch at this stage in the 2018 midterm elections, a Yahoo Finance review found. That election eight years ago was the last time Trump faced midterm voters and also saw him tout projects — most notably a Foxconn electronics manufacturing plant planned for Wisconsin — that turned out to be less than advertised. President Trump shakes hands with then-Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker at a groundbreaking for a Foxconn plant on June 28, 2018, in Mount Pleasant, Wisc. (Brian Cassella/Chicago Tribune/Tribune News Service via Getty Images) Chicago Tribune via Getty Images "FoxConn … had a ribbon-cutting a few months ago," Trump said at a stop in Wisconsin on the eve of the 2018 election , pledging that the project was set to bring in "almost 15,000 jobs and there is no plant like it in the United States." But the company eventually scrapped much of its manufacturing plans at the site and shifted the focus to data centers. Today, it employs only a reported 1,200 people at the site. The president's penchant for promises is on display again as Election Day nears. On Tuesday, he is set to travel to Alaska to tout a proposed $50 billion gas pipeline between South Korea and Alaska that could help Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan fend off a Democratic challenge. Trump unveiled the project earlier this month in the Oval Office with Sullivan at his side, but South Korean officials immediately pushed back, saying no final investment decision has been made . Korean President Lee Jae Myung even added that the deal will only proceed once the project's "commercial viability is confirmed." President Trump listens to Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) during an announcement at the White House in September. (Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images) KENT NISHIMURA via Getty Images Trump's promises in recent weeks have also included a $4 billion aluminum processing plant in Oklahoma . But local opposition to that plan — citing possible toxic chemicals and rising electricity prices — has led the town's mayor and a board of trustees to pause zoning approvals, leaving the fate of the project up in the air. Even the project's developers recently reported to the SEC that "to complete this project, we will need to obtain substantial additional financing, and there can be no assurance that such financing will be available." That didn't slow Trump from saying earlier this month that it would be "the largest aluminum factory, perhaps in the world, and you're going to make a fortune with it, lots of jobs, a lot of everything." A record of Trump overstating his own role The 2018 campaign was also notable for Trump overstating his role in various projects. In 2018, Trump often mentioned Apple's plans to spend $350 billion in the US, which he said was happening "only" because of his tax cut. "We are making some of the biggest and most important deals in our country's history," Trump posted on his then-Twitter account at the time. Yet those claims were an inflation of Apple's investment promises — which totaled about $55 billion for 2018 — and the company said at the time that they were made not just for tax reasons. Apple has been adept at repackaging long-term investment promises for each administration, with overlapping pledges made during Trump's first term, the Biden administration, and then again as Trump returned to office. Apple chair Tim Cook, center, applauds as President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping arrive for a state dinner at the White House on Sept. 24. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images) BRENDAN SMIALOWSKI via Getty Images Trump has also focused on a recent announcement of plans for a new $15 billion steel plant in Iowa. Iowa's governor recently signed a bill to move forward with government incentives, but the steel plant's ultimate fate still raises questions, especially given that one of its financiers previously filed for Chapter 11 protection . Trump's track record stretching back to 2018 has drawn skepticism about those plans. Iowa's Democratic nominee for governor, Rob Sand, noted the benefits of a steel plant while also reportedly telling voters at one stop that they have reason to be skeptical of a promise "that gets rolled out right before an election." The example he pointed to? Foxconn. Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance.
